regions.name: Burgundy
regions.summary: Burgundy is one grape per colour read through place: Pinot Noir for red, Chardonnay for white. The Côte d'Or, a limestone slope from Dijon to Maranges, splits into the Côte de Nuits for red and the Côte de Beaune for both; Chablis sits alone to the north; the Côte Chalonnaise and the Mâconnais run south. The law ranks ground in four tiers, regional, village, premier cru and grand cru, and a grand cru stands on the label under its climat name alone. Holdings are small and split among heirs, so the grower's name matters as much as the vineyard's.

terroir.climate: Continental: cold winters, spring frost, summer hail and the chance of rain at harvest, so vintages differ sharply. Chablis is the coldest corner and loses crop to frost in a bad spring; the Mâconnais is warm enough for Chardonnay to ripen fuller and earlier.
terroir.soils: Jurassic limestone and marl throughout. Chablis lies on Kimmeridgian limestone marl full of fossil oysters, with Portlandian limestone on the plateau above for Petit Chablis. The Côte d'Or mixes limestone scree, marl and clay, heavier on the Côte de Nuits, lighter and chalkier around the great white villages.
terroir.topography: The Côte d'Or is a narrow escarpment facing east and south-east; the best vineyards sit mid-slope, above the frost that pools on the flat and below the thin-soiled hilltop. Chablis is rolling hill country on the Serein, and the Mâconnais ends under the limestone rocks of Solutré and Vergisson.
terroir.water: The Serein runs through Chablis and its right bank carries the grand crus. The Saône flows down the plain east of the Côte d'Or, too far off to moderate the slope; drainage rather than water shapes the sites.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Every red of the Côte d'Or and the Côte Chalonnaise: cherry, rose and earth on fine tannin, from supple village wine to grand crus that live for decades.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Steely and unoaked in Chablis, barrel-fermented and nutty on the Côte de Beaune, ripe and rounded in the Mâconnais; also the base of Crémant de Bourgogne.

grapes.name: Aligoté
grapes.styles: Lean, lemony white for Bourgogne Aligoté and the kir; Bouzeron is its one village appellation.

grapes.name: Gamay
grapes.styles: Blended with Pinot Noir in Bourgogne Passe-Tout-Grains and used for Mâcon rouge; its real home is Beaujolais.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Saint-Bris near Auxerre is its single Burgundy appellation.

wines.note: Steely, saline Chardonnay with green apple and oyster shell, usually unoaked; serve cold with oysters and raw shellfish.
Pinot Noir with cherry, rose, earth and fine tannin; decant the young, pour the mature with duck, lamb or mushrooms.
Meursault, Puligny and Chassagne: barrel-fermented Chardonnay with hazelnut, citrus and stone; serve at 11 to 13 °C with butter sauces and lobster.
Pommard sturdy, Volnay silky, Beaune and Savigny supple; premier cru is the ceiling for all of them.
Riper Chardonnay with peach and honeysuckle, usually unoaked at Mâcon-Villages, often barrel-aged at Pouilly-Fuissé.
Traditional method from Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Aligoté and Gamay, at least nine months on lees; a crisp aperitif.

made.viticulture: Vines are trained low on single Guyot or cordon de Royat and planted densely, around ten thousand to the hectare on the Côte d'Or, so each carries a small crop; the permitted yield falls as the tier rises. Spring frost is the first hazard, fought in Chablis with sprinklers that coat the buds in protective ice and with heaters along the rows; hail is the second, and rot in a wet September the third. Picking is by hand on the slopes, and organic and biodynamic farming is widespread. Inheritance split holdings across generations, so a grower may own a few rows in a dozen climats.
made.winemaking: Red Burgundy is Pinot Noir fermented in open vats after a cold soak, the cap punched down, with a choice over whole bunches: stems add spice and grip, destemming gives purer fruit. The wine ages in the 228 litre pièce, the share of new oak rising with the tier, for twelve to eighteen months. Chardonnay is pressed whole and fermented in barrel on the Côte de Beaune, kept on its lees with bâtonnage and taken through malolactic conversion, which softens the acid; lees and barrel give the hazelnut; Chablis more often ferments in steel or old wood to keep its edge. Chaptalisation is allowed within limits in cold years, and above the regional tier a label names the place and the grower, seldom the grape.

law.classification: Burgundy ranks ground, not estates. Regional appellations sit at the base; village appellations carry a commune name; premier cru adds a named climat after the village; grand cru stands under the climat name alone, as in Chambertin or Montrachet, and amounts to about one bottle in a hundred. There are thirty-three grand crus: twenty-four on the Côte de Nuits, eight on the Côte de Beaune and the single Chablis Grand Cru with its seven climats. The climats were inscribed by UNESCO in 2015. A wine may always be declassified downward, never promoted.
tiers: Régionale

Bourgogne, Bourgogne Aligoté, Bourgogne Passe-Tout-Grains, Coteaux Bourguignons, Bourgogne Hautes-Côtes de Nuits and de Beaune, Bourgogne Côte d'Or (from the 2017 vintage), Mâcon and Crémant de Bourgogne: about half of all Burgundy.
Village
A commune name on the label, Meursault or Gevrey-Chambertin; a named lieu-dit may follow in smaller type.
Premier Cru
Village plus climat, as in Beaune Premier Cru Clos des Mouches; a blend of several climats is simply village Premier Cru.
Grand Cru
The climat alone, no village name: Chambertin, Musigny, Corton-Charlemagne. Chablis Grand Cru carries its climat after the appellation.
labels: A named, delimited vineyard parcel; the unit on which the whole hierarchy rests.
A climat in a single owner's hands, such as La Tâche or Clos de Tart.
A domaine bottles its own vineyards; a maison or négociant buys grapes or wine and bottles under its own name.
The charitable hospital founded in 1443, whose wines sell at auction each November.
Old vines; the term is unregulated.

places.name: Chablis
places.note: Chardonnay alone on Kimmeridgian marl around the Serein, cold and frost-prone: steely, saline wine that rarely sees new oak, in four tiers.

places.name: Petit Chablis
places.note: The outer plateau on Portlandian limestone: light, sharp and for early drinking.

places.name: Chablis Premier Cru
places.note: Named climats on both banks: Montée de Tonnerre, Fourchaume and Mont de Milieu on the right, Vaillons and Montmains on the left.

places.name: Chablis Grand Cru
places.note: One appellation, seven climats on one south-west facing slope above the town: Blanchot, Bougros, Les Clos, Grenouilles, Preuses, Valmur and Vaudésir; Les Clos is the most famous.

places.name: Saint-Bris
places.note: Sauvignon Blanc's only Burgundy appellation, since 2003, near Auxerre.

places.name: Irancy
places.note: Pinot Noir red near Auxerre that may carry a little of the local César.

places.name: Côte de Nuits
places.note: The northern half of the Côte d'Or, Marsannay to Corgoloin: almost all Pinot Noir, twenty-four grand crus, and the firmest, longest-lived red Burgundy.

places.name: Marsannay
places.note: The northern gateway, a village appellation since 1987 and the only one with its own rosé.

places.name: Gevrey-Chambertin
places.note: The largest village of the Côte de Nuits and home of nine grand crus, every one carrying the name Chambertin: deep, powerful, earthy Pinot Noir.

places.name: Chambertin and Chambertin-Clos de Bèze
places.note: The two great crus at the heart of the slope; Clos de Bèze may be sold as Chambertin, never the reverse.

places.name: The seven other Chambertins
places.note: Chapelle, Charmes, Griotte, Latricières, Mazis, Mazoyères and Ruchottes, each hyphenated to Chambertin; Mazoyères may be sold as Charmes.

places.name: Clos Saint-Jacques
places.note: A premier cru prized and priced as a grand cru.

places.name: Morey-Saint-Denis
places.note: Between Gevrey and Chambolle: Clos de la Roche, Clos Saint-Denis, Clos des Lambrays, the monopole Clos de Tart and a slice of Bonnes-Mares.

places.name: Chambolle-Musigny
places.note: The most perfumed, silkiest reds; grand crus Musigny and Bonnes-Mares, and Les Amoureuses, the premier cru that drinks like one.

places.name: Musigny
places.note: Chambolle's crown and the only grand cru of the Côte de Nuits permitted to make white.

places.name: Vougeot
places.note: Dominated by the walled Clos de Vougeot, enclosed by Cistercian monks and now split among scores of owners, so the grower is everything.

places.name: Flagey-Échezeaux
places.note: Holds the grand crus Échezeaux and Grands Échezeaux; its village wine is sold as Vosne-Romanée.

places.name: Vosne-Romanée
places.note: Six grand crus in one village, Romanée-Conti, La Tâche, La Romanée, Richebourg, Romanée-Saint-Vivant and La Grande Rue: spice, silk and length.

places.name: Romanée-Conti and La Tâche
places.note: Both monopoles of the Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, which has held Romanée-Conti since 1869.

places.name: La Romanée
places.note: The smallest grand cru appellation in France, a monopole just above Romanée-Conti.

places.name: Nuits-Saint-Georges
places.note: Firm, earthy, tannic reds with no grand cru; premier crus Les Saint-Georges, Les Vaucrains, Les Pruliers and Les Cailles lie to the south.

places.name: Côte de Beaune
places.note: The southern half of the Côte d'Or, Ladoix to Maranges: the great whites of Meursault, Puligny and Chassagne, Corton as its lone red grand cru, and supple reds capped at premier cru.

places.name: The hill of Corton
places.note: Shared by Aloxe-Corton, Ladoix-Serrigny and Pernand-Vergelesses. Corton, red with a little white, is the Côte d'Or's largest grand cru; Corton-Charlemagne is the white of its upper slopes.

places.name: Savigny-lès-Beaune
places.note: Supple, early-drinking reds and some white, with premier crus such as Les Lavières and Les Vergelesses; Chorey-lès-Beaune on the flat below has none.

places.name: Beaune
places.note: The merchant capital and seat of the Hospices; no grand cru but premier crus Grèves, Clos des Mouches, Clos de la Mousse, Bressandes and Teurons.

places.name: Pommard
places.note: The sturdiest Côte de Beaune red, tannic and iron-edged; Les Rugiens and Les Épenots lead, and Clos des Épeneaux is a monopole.

places.name: Volnay
places.note: Pommard's silky, perfumed neighbour; Clos des Ducs is a monopole, Caillerets and Champans the names to know, Santenots its red grown in Meursault.

places.name: Monthelie, Auxey-Duresses and Saint-Romain
places.note: Side-valley villages behind Volnay and Meursault: lighter, sharper, good value.

places.name: Meursault
places.note: The largest white village: rich, nutty, barrel-fermented Chardonnay with no grand cru; premier crus Perrières, Genevrières and Charmes, and high lieux-dits such as Les Tillets.

places.name: Puligny-Montrachet
places.note: The most precise white village: Montrachet and Bâtard-Montrachet shared with Chassagne, Chevalier-Montrachet and Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet its own; premier crus Les Pucelles and Les Combettes.

places.name: Montrachet
places.note: The most celebrated dry white vineyard in the world, straddling the village boundary.

places.name: Chassagne-Montrachet
places.note: White and red; holds Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet and its shares of Montrachet and Bâtard, with premier crus Morgeot and Caillerets.

places.name: Saint-Aubin
places.note: Up the side valley behind Puligny: taut, mineral white premier crus such as Le Charmois and En Remilly.

places.name: Santenay and Maranges
places.note: The southern end of the slope: honest reds, some white, premier crus but no grand cru.

places.name: Côte Chalonnaise
places.note: South of the Côte d'Or without its unbroken slope: lighter Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, premier crus and no grand cru.

places.name: Bouzeron
places.note: The one village appellation for Aligoté, created in 1997.

places.name: Rully
places.note: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and a centre of Crémant de Bourgogne.

places.name: Mercurey
places.note: The largest Chalonnaise village, mostly firm Pinot Noir with premier crus.

places.name: Givry
places.note: Pinot Noir of charm with a small amount of white.

places.name: Montagny
places.note: Chardonnay only, the southernmost Chalonnaise village, with premier crus.

places.name: Mâconnais
places.note: Burgundy's largest source of Chardonnay: rolling limestone hills north of Beaujolais, warmer and riper, mostly white.

places.name: Mâcon and Mâcon-Villages
places.note: Mâcon-Villages is white only; a commune may hang its name on Mâcon, as at Mâcon-Igé, and the hill villages west of the town are the best.

places.name: Verzé
places.note: Hill village selling white as Mâcon-Verzé, where a great Puligny domaine now farms.

places.name: Milly-Lamartine
places.note: Neighbouring hill village of Mâcon-Milly-Lamartine, farmed by a famous Meursault family.

places.name: Viré-Clessé
places.note: A village appellation since 1999 from two merged communes: ripe Chardonnay, occasionally late-picked.

places.name: Pouilly-Fuissé
places.note: The flagship, under the rocks of Solutré and Vergisson across four villages: barrel-aged Chardonnay, and twenty-two premier cru climats recognised by the INAO on 3 September 2020, from that vintage.

places.name: Pouilly-Loché and Pouilly-Vinzelles
places.note: Two small neighbours of Pouilly-Fuissé; Loché may be sold as Vinzelles. Four premier cru climats, one in Loché and three in Vinzelles, were published by the INAO in November 2024 and apply from the 2024 vintage.

places.name: Saint-Véran
places.note: Wraps Pouilly-Fuissé on both sides: fresh Chardonnay, often a good buy.

producers.name: Domaine de la Romanée-Conti
producers.why: The most famous domaine in the world, with the monopoles Romanée-Conti and La Tâche.

producers.name: Domaine Leroy
producers.why: Biodynamic Vosne-Romanée estate whose wines rank with the Romanée-Conti among Burgundy's most sought after.

producers.name: Domaine Armand Rousseau
producers.why: Gevrey-Chambertin's great name: Chambertin, Clos de Bèze and the premier cru Clos Saint-Jacques.

producers.name: Domaine Georges Roumier
producers.why: Chambolle-Musigny benchmark, with the monopole Clos de la Bussière in Morey-Saint-Denis.

producers.name: Comte Georges de Vogüé
producers.why: The largest holder of Musigny and the historic maker of its rare white.

producers.name: Domaine Henri Gouges
producers.why: The reference for Nuits-Saint-Georges premier crus such as Les Pruliers and Les Saint-Georges.

producers.name: Domaine Jean Grivot
producers.why: Vosne-Romanée domaine with Échezeaux and Richebourg and village wines that age well.

producers.name: Domaine des Comtes Lafon
producers.why: Meursault's standard-setter, including the walled Clos de la Barre and the Mâcon arm, Les Héritiers du Comte Lafon.

producers.name: Coche-Dury
producers.why: Among the most sought-after white Burgundy estates, from Bourgogne Blanc up to Corton-Charlemagne.

producers.name: Domaine Roulot
producers.why: Meursault lieux-dits and premier crus of precision and tension.

producers.name: Domaine Leflaive
producers.why: Puligny-Montrachet's most famous domaine, biodynamic, with Chevalier-Montrachet and a Mâcon-Verzé arm.

producers.name: Domaine Marquis d'Angerville
producers.why: Volnay's monopole Clos des Ducs and the estate that fought for domaine bottling in the 1930s.

producers.name: Domaine Tollot-Beaut
producers.why: Chorey-lès-Beaune domaine known for ripe Savigny and Beaune premier crus.

producers.name: Domaine Paul Pillot
producers.why: Chassagne-Montrachet grower with a fine Saint-Aubin Le Charmois.

producers.name: François Carillon
producers.why: Puligny-Montrachet from one of the village's oldest growing families.

producers.name: Domaine Raveneau
producers.why: The cult name in Chablis, premier and grand crus raised in old wood.

producers.name: Domaine Vincent Dauvissat
producers.why: Chablis grower of Les Preuses and Les Clos with the same old-barrel discipline as Raveneau.

producers.name: Domaine Louis Michel
producers.why: The clearest case for unoaked Chablis, steel at every tier.

producers.name: Jean-Paul et Benoît Droin
producers.why: Chablis family domaine with a broad run of premier crus including Vaillons.

producers.name: Maison Louis Jadot
producers.why: Beaune négociant and domaine across the whole region, from Beaune premier crus to Meursault and Beaujolais.

producers.name: Maison Joseph Drouhin
producers.why: Beaune house whose Clos des Mouches premier cru is a famous name in both colours.

producers.name: Bouchard Père et Fils
producers.why: Historic Beaune négociant with the monopole Clos de la Mousse and Vigne de l'Enfant Jésus.

producers.name: Domaine Faiveley
producers.why: Nuits-Saint-Georges house with holdings from Chambertin to Mercurey; its Bourgogne Rouge is a model entry wine.

producers.name: Domaine du Roc des Boutires
producers.why: Single-parcel Pouilly-Fuissé that shows the Mâconnais at its most serious.

producers.name: Domaine Fichet
producers.why: Mâcon-Igé grower whose Chardonnay is a model of the hill villages.

producers.name: Domaine A. et P. de Villaine
producers.why: The Bouzeron domaine that made Aligoté respectable.

exam: The four tiers and how each reads on a label.
Which villages hold which grand crus, and which famous villages have none.
Chablis: Kimmeridgian soil, seven grand cru climats, the unoaked default.
The Mâconnais and Côte Chalonnaise appellations and their grapes.
Négociant against domaine, and the words that tell them apart.
Pouilly-Fuissé against Pouilly-Fumé, every single time.
traps: Pouilly-Fuissé is Mâconnais Chardonnay; Pouilly-Fumé is Loire Sauvignon Blanc.
Nuits-Saint-Georges, Beaune, Pommard, Volnay and Meursault have no grand cru.
Corton is the only red grand cru of the Côte de Beaune; Musigny the only white of the Côte de Nuits.
Chablis Grand Cru is one appellation with seven climats; Les Clos is a climat, not a village.
A grand cru label carries no village name; a premier cru carries both.
Bourgogne Côte d'Or is a regional appellation, not a village one.
Mâconnais premier crus are Pouilly-Fuissé's, from the 2020 vintage, and since the 2024 vintage four in Pouilly-Loché and Pouilly-Vinzelles; none elsewhere as of the 2024 vintage.

cards.f: The four tiers of Burgundy, bottom to top
cards.b: Regional (Bourgogne), village (Meursault), premier cru (village plus climat), grand cru (the climat alone on the label: Chambertin).

cards.f: Grand crus of Chablis: how many, and name them
cards.b: Seven climats in one appellation: Blanchot, Bougros, Les Clos, Grenouilles, Preuses, Valmur, Vaudésir.

cards.f: The nine grand crus of Gevrey-Chambertin
cards.b: Chambertin, Chambertin-Clos de Bèze, Chapelle, Charmes, Griotte, Latricières, Mazis, Mazoyères and Ruchottes, all suffixed Chambertin.
Romanée-Conti, La Tâche, La Romanée, Richebourg, Romanée-Saint-Vivant, La Grande Rue; Échezeaux and Grands Échezeaux lie next door in Flagey.

cards.f: The only red grand cru of the Côte de Beaune
cards.b: Corton, on the hill shared by Aloxe-Corton, Ladoix-Serrigny and Pernand-Vergelesses; Corton-Charlemagne is its white.

cards.f: Famous villages with no grand cru
cards.b: Nuits-Saint-Georges, Beaune, Pommard, Volnay and Meursault: premier cru is their ceiling.
Fuissé is Mâconnais Chardonnay under the rock of Solutré; Fumé is Loire Sauvignon Blanc on flint.
A regional red blending Gamay with Pinot Noir: Pinot Noir must be at least 30 per cent of the blend and Gamay at least 15 per cent.
Kimmeridgian limestone marl with fossil oysters under the crus; Portlandian limestone on the higher Petit Chablis plateau.

cards.f: The count of grand crus in Burgundy
cards.b: Thirty-three: twenty-four on the Côte de Nuits, eight on the Côte de Beaune, one in Chablis.

questions.q: Which village holds the grand cru La Tâche?
questions.exp: La Tâche is one of the six grand crus of Vosne-Romanée and a monopole of the Domaine de la Romanée-Conti. Gevrey has the Chambertins, Chambolle has Musigny and Morey the four clos.

questions.q: Which of these Côte de Beaune villages has no grand cru vineyard?
questions.exp: Volnay, like Pommard, Beaune and Meursault, tops out at premier cru. Aloxe-Corton holds Corton and Corton-Charlemagne; Puligny and Chassagne share Montrachet and Bâtard-Montrachet and each holds grand crus of its own.

questions.q: On which geological formation do the premier and grand cru vineyards of Chablis lie?
questions.exp: The crus sit on Kimmeridgian limestone marl rich in fossil oysters. Portlandian limestone caps the plateau and carries Petit Chablis; the other two are Jurassic stages found elsewhere.

questions.q: How many grand cru climats share the single Chablis Grand Cru appellation?
questions.exp: Blanchot, Bougros, Les Clos, Grenouilles, Preuses, Valmur and Vaudésir make seven, all on one slope on the right bank of the Serein.

questions.q: Which grand cru of the Côte de Nuits may also be made as a white wine?
questions.exp: Musigny alone among the Côte de Nuits grand crus permits a white, a tiny Chardonnay bottling. The others are red only.

questions.q: Aligoté has one village appellation of its own in Burgundy. Name it.
questions.exp: Bouzeron, in the Côte Chalonnaise, became a village appellation for Aligoté in 1997; everywhere else the grape is sold as Bourgogne Aligoté.

questions.q: Which regional appellation must blend at least 30 per cent Pinot Noir with at least 15 per cent Gamay?
questions.exp: Passe-Tout-Grains is the blend with fixed floors: at least 30 per cent Pinot Noir and 15 per cent Gamay. Coteaux Bourguignons may blend the two in any share.

questions.q: Which Mâconnais appellation became the first in its sub-region to carry premier cru climats, from the 2020 vintage?
questions.exp: The INAO recognised twenty-two premier cru climats for Pouilly-Fuissé on 3 September 2020, a mention added to the appellation rather than a separate one.

regions.name: Beaujolais
regions.summary: Beaujolais is Gamay on granite, a run of hills between the Mâconnais and Lyon that belongs to greater Burgundy in law and tastes nothing like it. The ten crus occupy the granite and schist of the north, from Saint-Amour down to Brouilly, and none of them need print the word Beaujolais on the label; Beaujolais-Villages covers the hamlets around them and plain Beaujolais the clay and limestone of the south. Whole bunches fermented under carbon dioxide give the light, fruity style; the crus, made more like red Burgundy, can age. Serve it lightly chilled, and remember Nouveau arrives on the third Thursday of November.

terroir.climate: Continental, a touch warmer than the Côte d'Or and open to Mediterranean warmth from the south, so Gamay ripens fully; summer hail and spring frost on the lower ground are the hazards, and the Monts du Beaujolais shelter the slopes from western rain.
terroir.soils: Pink granite and schist in the north, weathering to the coarse sand the crus prize; the hard blue stone, the pierre bleue, of Mont Brouilly, manganese-rich granite at Moulin-à-Vent, decomposed schist on the Côte du Py. South of Villefranche the ground turns to clay and the golden limestone of the Pierres Dorées, home of plain Beaujolais.
terroir.topography: Hills rising west of the Saône plain to the forested Monts du Beaujolais, the crus on east and south-east facing slopes between about 200 and 500 metres; Chiroubles is the highest cru and the lightest.
terroir.water: The Saône flows past on the eastern plain and the small Nizerand marks the rough divide between the granite north and the limestone south.

grapes.name: Gamay
grapes.styles: Nearly the whole vineyard: cherry, raspberry and violet, light tannin and bright acid, from carbonic Nouveau to cru wines that age like Burgundy.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: The grape of Beaujolais Blanc, grown mostly in the north near the Mâconnais border.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Long allowed as a small accessory share in the red and little seen; Beaujolais is Gamay's region, not Pinot's.

wines.note: Bottled weeks after harvest and released on the third Thursday of November: banana, bubblegum and cherry from carbonic maceration, served cool and drunk young.
Light, juicy, low-tannin reds for charcuterie, roast chicken and the bistro table; serve at cellar temperature, around 13 °C.
Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent dense and ageworthy, Fleurie and Chiroubles perfumed and silky; the serious glass that pairs with duck, pork and mushrooms.
Chardonnay, crisp and modest, from the northern fringe; a cousin of Mâcon-Villages.
Gamay rosé, pale and strawberry-scented, made in small amounts for summer.

made.viticulture: Gamay was banished from the Côte d'Or by a ducal edict of 1395 and found its true home on this granite, where its vigour is checked by poor sandy soil. The traditional training is the gobelet, a free-standing bush that suits the warm slopes and the hand picking that whole-bunch fermentation demands; cordon and Guyot are now also permitted. Vine density is high, at least six thousand to the hectare, and yields are capped more tightly for the crus than for Villages and plain Beaujolais. Harvest comes early for Burgundy, late August into September, and the whole region picks fast because Nouveau must be in bottle within weeks. Hail is the enemy of the hillside crus, and the sandy soils drain so quickly that drought now matters more than rot. A growing number of estates farm organically, and the old gobelet vines of Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent are the source of the region's longest-lived wines.
made.winemaking: Whole bunches go uncrushed into a vat that is sealed and often filled with carbon dioxide. In full carbonic maceration the berries ferment from the inside, without yeast contact, producing little tannin and the banana and bubblegum esters of Nouveau; the grapes are pressed after a few days and the juice finishes fermenting off the skins. Semi-carbonic is the norm: the bottom of the vat crushes under its own weight and ferments conventionally, releasing the gas that protects the intact berries above. The crus are increasingly made like red Burgundy, destemmed or whole-bunch with a longer maceration, punched down and aged in older oak foudres or barrels so they gain structure and keep. A natural-wine school rooted in Morgon in the 1980s revived long, cool whole-bunch ferments with native yeasts and little or no added sulphur, and its influence runs through the crus today. Beaujolais Blanc is made as a simple unoaked Chardonnay.

law.classification: Three tiers, all under Gamay. Beaujolais AOC covers the whole region, its heart the clay and limestone of the south; Beaujolais-Villages takes in the granite hamlets of the north that sit outside the crus; and the ten crus, Saint-Amour, Juliénas, Chénas, Moulin-à-Vent, Fleurie, Chiroubles, Morgon, Régnié, Côte de Brouilly and Brouilly, each has its own appellation and need not print the word Beaujolais. Nouveau and Primeur may be made as Beaujolais or Beaujolais-Villages, never as a cru. The region sits in the Rhône département for the most part, with Saint-Amour across the line in Saône-et-Loire, and in law it belongs to greater Burgundy, so a cru's Gamay may be sold as Bourgogne Gamay.
tiers: Beaujolais
The regional base: red from Gamay, white from Chardonnay, a little rosé; Nouveau is sold at this tier.
Beaujolais-Villages
The named hamlets of the northern granite, outside the crus; firmer and riper than plain Beaujolais; may also be Nouveau.
Cru
Ten village appellations on the northern granite, red only, with no need of the word Beaujolais on the label; no Nouveau.
labels: Wine released the third Thursday of November, weeks after harvest.
The famous schist hill of Morgon, named on labels as a climat.
Old vines, unregulated, common on the crus.
The regional Burgundy label a cru's Gamay may take when declassified.

places.name: Southern Beaujolais and the Pierres Dorées
places.note: The clay and golden limestone country south of Villefranche: plain Beaujolais, light and simple, and the source of most Nouveau.

places.name: Beaujolais-Villages
places.note: The granite hamlets of the north outside the ten crus, riper and firmer than plain Beaujolais; the middle tier and a sound bistro pour.

places.name: The ten crus
places.note: All on the granite and schist north of Villefranche, each a village appellation in its own right, listed here north to south.

places.name: Saint-Amour
places.note: The northernmost cru, across the line in Saône-et-Loire; light, floral and popular on one day in February.

places.name: Juliénas
places.note: Firm, spicy wines on granite and schist with clay to the east; one of the sturdier crus.

places.name: Chénas
places.note: The smallest cru, named for the oaks that once stood there; structured wines close to Moulin-à-Vent in style.

places.name: Moulin-à-Vent
places.note: Named for the windmill above Romanèche-Thorins; manganese-streaked granite gives the deepest, most tannic cru, one that can age ten years and taste like Burgundy.

places.name: Fleurie
places.note: Pink granite and the most perfumed cru: violets, raspberry and silk; the Clos de la Roilette lies on its border with Moulin-à-Vent.

places.name: Chiroubles
places.note: The highest cru, on sandy granite: the lightest and most delicate, drunk young.

places.name: Morgon
places.note: Around Villié-Morgon, one of the largest crus and with Moulin-à-Vent the most ageworthy; cherry and kirsch that turn earthy with age, a change the locals call morgonner.

places.name: Côte du Py
places.note: The hill of decomposed schist above Villié-Morgon, the cru's grandest site and the birthplace of its natural-wine school.

places.name: Régnié
places.note: Promoted in 1988, the most recent of the ten crus as of 2026, on pink granite sand: light, fruity and early drinking.

places.name: Côte de Brouilly
places.note: The steep slopes of Mont Brouilly, a hill of hard blue-green stone the growers call pierre bleue: riper and more concentrated than the Brouilly that surrounds it.

places.name: Brouilly
places.note: The largest and southernmost cru, ringing the mountain on mixed granite and limestone: supple, fruity and generous.

producers.name: Jean Foillard
producers.why: Morgon Côte du Py from the natural-wine school: whole bunches, cool ferments, old foudres.

producers.name: Marcel Lapierre
producers.why: The Morgon domaine at the root of natural Beaujolais, silky and pure.

producers.name: Domaine Coudert
producers.why: Fleurie's Clos de la Roilette, on the Moulin-à-Vent border, juicy and built to keep.

producers.name: Château des Jacques
producers.why: Moulin-à-Vent estate in Jadot's hands that makes cru Beaujolais the Burgundian way, by named climat.

producers.name: Château Thivin
producers.why: The reference for Côte de Brouilly from the slopes of Mont Brouilly.

producers.name: Georges Duboeuf
producers.why: The négociant of Romanèche-Thorins who turned Nouveau into a worldwide event.

producers.name: Maison Louis Jadot
producers.why: The Beaune house whose Beaujolais-Villages is a dependable glass of the middle tier.

exam: The ten crus by name, and that a cru need not say Beaujolais on the label.
Carbonic and semi-carbonic maceration, and what they do to Gamay.
Granite in the north, clay and limestone in the south.
Nouveau: the day, the tier and the method.
The crus to cellar against the crus to drink young.
traps: A cru label need not carry the word Beaujolais; Beaujolais-Villages always does.
Nouveau may be Beaujolais or Beaujolais-Villages, never a cru.
Côte de Brouilly and Brouilly are two crus: the hill and the ring around it.
Beaujolais is in greater Burgundy by law; the grape is Gamay, not Pinot Noir.
Carbonic maceration is a fermentation method, not a grape or a place.
Régnié joined the crus in 1988; there have been ten ever since, not nine or twelve.

cards.f: The ten crus of Beaujolais, north to south
cards.b: Saint-Amour, Juliénas, Chénas, Moulin-à-Vent, Fleurie, Chiroubles, Morgon, Régnié, Côte de Brouilly, Brouilly.

cards.f: The grape of Beaujolais and its rock
cards.b: Gamay on granite and schist in the north; clay and limestone in the south for plain Beaujolais.

cards.f: Beaujolais Nouveau: release day and method
cards.b: The third Thursday of November; carbonic or semi-carbonic maceration gives banana and bubblegum scents.
Beaujolais, Beaujolais-Villages, then the ten crus, which need not print the word Beaujolais.
Moulin-à-Vent and Morgon; Morgon's Côte du Py is the famous schist hill.
Chiroubles, the highest, and Fleurie; Saint-Amour and Régnié are light too.
Chardonnay, mostly from the northern fringe by the Mâconnais.
Lightly chilled, around 13 to 14 °C; Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent with a few years take a brief decant.

questions.q: Which cru is the largest of the ten by vineyard area?
questions.exp: Brouilly, ringing Mont Brouilly at the southern end of the cru zone, is the biggest; Morgon is the other large one, Fleurie mid-sized and Chiroubles among the smallest.

questions.q: Which cru was the last to be added to the list, in 1988?
questions.exp: Régnié was promoted from Beaujolais-Villages in 1988, making the crus ten. The other three had held cru status since the 1930s and 1940s.

questions.q: On which day is Beaujolais Nouveau released each year?
questions.exp: Nouveau is released at one minute past midnight on the third Thursday of November, weeks after harvest, as Beaujolais or Beaujolais-Villages.

questions.q: Which cru takes in the steep slopes of the blue-stone hill at the southern end of the cru zone, with a larger cru ringing its foot?
questions.exp: Côte de Brouilly is the hill itself, Mont Brouilly, whose hard blue-green stone gives riper, more concentrated wine; Brouilly is the larger, flatter cru around its foot. The two are separate appellations.

questions.q: Name the hill of decomposed schist above Villié-Morgon that is Morgon's most famous site.
questions.exp: The Côte du Py is a hill of decomposed schist that gives Morgon's deepest, most ageworthy wine and appears on labels as a climat.

questions.q: What is the whole-bunch fermentation in a sealed, carbon-dioxide-filled vat that gives Nouveau its banana and bubblegum scent?
questions.exp: Carbonic maceration ferments intact berries from within, extracting colour and fruit esters but little tannin; most Beaujolais is made by the semi-carbonic variant.

questions.q: Which grape makes the white wine labelled Beaujolais Blanc?
questions.exp: Beaujolais Blanc is Chardonnay, grown mostly on the limestone fringe near the Mâconnais; Gamay is the region's red grape only.

questions.q: Which cru is held, with Morgon, to be the most structured and longest-lived of the ten?
questions.exp: Moulin-à-Vent's manganese-streaked granite gives the firmest, most tannic Gamay, a wine that can age ten years and taste like Burgundy; Chiroubles, Saint-Amour and Régnié are light crus for early drinking.

regions.name: Rhône Valley
regions.summary: The Rhône is two regions on one river. North of a fifty kilometre gap below Valence the climate is continental, the slopes steep granite, and Syrah is the only black grape, with Viognier at Condrieu and Marsanne and Roussanne for the other whites; the crus run from Côte-Rôtie to Cornas and Saint-Péray. South of the gap the valley widens into Mediterranean country where bush-trained Grenache leads blends with Syrah and Mourvèdre, crowned by Châteauneuf-du-Pape and its thirteen named grapes. Labels climb from Côtes du Rhône through Villages to the crus, which drop the regional name; Tavel is rosé only and two villages fortify sweet wine.

terroir.climate: Continental in the north, with cold winters, warm summers and vintage swings; Mediterranean in the south, hot, dry and sunny, with most rain in autumn storms. The mistral blows down the whole valley, cold and dry, drying canopies, cutting rot and stressing the vines.
terroir.soils: Granite, gneiss and schist in the north, weathered to thin sandy soils on terraces; the Côte Brune of Côte-Rôtie holds iron-rich schist, the Côte Blonde lighter granite and gneiss. The south mixes the galets roulés of Châteauneuf, river-rounded quartzite stones over red clay, with sand, limestone scree under the Dentelles de Montmirail and gravel.
terroir.topography: The north is a narrow corridor of terraces cut into slopes so steep that dry-stone walls hold the soil and each vine may be tied to its own stake; Hermitage is a single hill on the east bank, granite at its core. The south opens into a broad plain and low hills, with the jagged limestone Dentelles above Gigondas and Mont Ventoux to the east.
terroir.water: The Rhône itself, whose ancient bed left the galets on the plateau of La Crau; the Isère at the edge of Crozes-Hermitage, the Drôme in the Diois, the Ouvèze below Gigondas and the Durance in the Luberon.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: The sole black grape of the north: black pepper, violet, olive and smoked meat on firm tannin, from Côte-Rôtie's perfume to Cornas's rugged depth; a blending partner for colour and spice in the south.

grapes.name: Grenache
grapes.styles: The backbone of the south: raspberry, kirsch, garrigue and warmth, bush-trained in Châteauneuf, Gigondas and Côtes du Rhône, and fortified as Rasteau.

grapes.name: Mourvèdre
grapes.styles: Late-ripening and tannic, adding meat, structure and keeping power to southern blends; a lead at some Châteauneuf estates.

grapes.name: Viognier
grapes.styles: Apricot, honeysuckle and oily weight at Condrieu and Château-Grillet; up to a fifth co-fermented into Côte-Rôtie.

grapes.name: Marsanne
grapes.styles: The northern white workhorse: honeysuckle, quince and waxy weight in Hermitage Blanc, Saint-Joseph, Crozes and Saint-Péray.

grapes.name: Roussanne
grapes.styles: Marsanne's aromatic partner, finer and harder to grow; a white Châteauneuf grape too.

grapes.name: Cinsault
grapes.styles: Soft red fruit and freshness in southern blends; a mainstay of Tavel rosé.

grapes.name: Carignan
grapes.styles: An accessory grape in Côtes du Rhône blends, capped by the rules.

grapes.name: Muscat Blanc
grapes.styles: The grape of the fortified Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise and the sweet sparkling Clairette de Die.

grapes.name: Counoise
grapes.styles: A peppery Châteauneuf variety, prized by a few estates for spice and acidity.

grapes.name: Clairette
grapes.styles: A southern white with soft acid, the lead of Gigondas white and a partner in white Châteauneuf.

wines.note: Syrah with a little Viognier co-fermented: violet, bacon, pepper and silk; decant young, pour with lamb or game birds.
The hill of power: dense, smoky, long-lived Syrah; the white, mostly Marsanne, is rich and ages for decades.
All Syrah and only red: rugged, dark and tannic when young, savoury and leathery with age.
Dry Viognier of apricot, honeysuckle and oily texture, low in acid; drink young at 10 to 12 °C with lobster or roast chicken.
Grenache-led, warm and spicy, raspberry and garrigue on soft tannin, in the embossed papal bottle; braised meats, lamb and strong cheeses.
Juicy Grenache-Syrah blends for everyday pouring; Villages is riper and more structured.
Dark, dry, full rosé from Grenache and Cinsault; the one cru that is rosé alone, for charcuterie and grilled fish.
Sweet, grapey vin doux naturel, fermentation stopped with spirit; serve cold with fruit desserts.

made.viticulture: Northern vines grow on terraces so steep that almost all work is by hand, and Syrah is trained on single wooden stakes, échalas, or on two crossed poles against the mistral; the walls need endless repair. Yields are low and harvest, from September, is by hand. In the south Grenache is grown as a low gobelet bush, pruned short so it withstands wind and drought, with Syrah on wires; Châteauneuf-du-Pape requires hand harvest and sorting of the crop, and sets its minimum alcohol at 12.5 per cent with no chaptalisation. The mistral dries the canopy and keeps fungal disease rare, which is why organic farming is so widespread in the south, but it also shreds shoots and can cut the crop. The galets of La Crau store the day's heat and release it at night, and sand such as that under Rayas gives a lighter, more perfumed Grenache. White vines were long interplanted among the black in the north and picked together, which is the root of the co-fermentation rules.
made.winemaking: Northern Syrah is often fermented with a share of whole bunches, the stems adding pepper and structure, and the permitted white grapes go into the vat with the black and ferment there, never blended in afterwards: up to twenty per cent Viognier at Côte-Rôtie, fifteen per cent Marsanne and Roussanne at Hermitage and Crozes-Hermitage, ten per cent at Saint-Joseph, none at Cornas. Ageing is in larger old barrels or demi-muids, with new oak a house choice rather than a rule. Southern reds are blends assembled after fermentation, Grenache usually raised in concrete or large foudres because it oxidises easily in small new wood, Syrah and Mourvèdre sometimes in barrel. The whites are mostly unoaked and drunk young, Hermitage Blanc the exception. The vins doux naturels of Beaumes-de-Venise and Rasteau are made by mutage, grape spirit added during fermentation to leave natural sugar. Tavel is a rosé of short maceration or saignée, deeper than Provence; Clairette de Die finishes its single fermentation in bottle by the ancestral method, and Saint-Péray and Crémant de Die use the traditional one.

law.classification: The valley carries one ladder. Côtes du Rhône, the base, covers both zones though nearly all of it is southern; Côtes du Rhône Villages demands lower yields and a higher share of Grenache; a Villages wine from a listed commune may add that name, Séguret or Sablet; and the crus, eight in the north and, with Laudun, ten in the south, stand under their own names with no mention of the Rhône. Two vins doux naturels and the Diois sparkling appellations sit alongside, with Ventoux, Luberon, Costières de Nîmes and Grignan-les-Adhémar as the satellites. The crus have grown: Vinsobres in 2006, Rasteau for dry wine in 2010, Cairanne from the 2015 vintage, and Laudun, approved by the INAO on 11 September 2024 for red and white from that vintage.
tiers: Côtes du Rhône
The regional base, red white and rosé; in the southern zone the rules ask the red for at least 30 per cent Grenache, with Syrah and Mourvèdre together at least 20 per cent.
Côtes du Rhône Villages
A tighter zone with lower yields; red at least half Grenache with Syrah and Mourvèdre at least a fifth.
Villages with a named commune
Villages wine from one of the listed communes, Séguret, Sablet, Valréas, Visan, Plan de Dieu and the rest, with the name added.
Cru
An appellation in its own right that leaves the Rhône off the label: Côte-Rôtie to Saint-Péray in the north, Châteauneuf-du-Pape to Laudun in the south.
labels: Sweet wine fortified during fermentation; Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise and Rasteau.
The rounded river stones of Châteauneuf-du-Pape that hold the day's heat.
The single stake each northern Syrah vine is tied to.
The two slopes of Côte-Rôtie: lighter granite and gneiss, and darker iron-rich schist.
The chapel on the hill of Hermitage and the Jaboulet wine named for it.
Straw wine of dried grapes, permitted at Hermitage.

places.name: Northern Rhône
places.note: The steep corridor from Vienne to Valence: Syrah alone for red, Viognier at Condrieu, Marsanne and Roussanne elsewhere, with granite under nearly everything.

places.name: Côte-Rôtie
places.note: The roasted slope above Ampuis, split into the Côte Blonde and the Côte Brune: Syrah with up to 20 per cent Viognier in the vat, the most perfumed northern red; Guigal's La Mouline, La Landonne and La Turque are its famous single vineyards.

places.name: Condrieu
places.note: Viognier only, nearly always dry, from granite terraces just south of Côte-Rôtie: apricot, honeysuckle and oil, for drinking young.

places.name: Château-Grillet
places.note: A single estate with its own appellation inside the Condrieu zone, Viognier from an amphitheatre of granite; one of France's smallest appellations.

places.name: Saint-Joseph
places.note: A long west-bank strip from Condrieu to Cornas, its heart around Mauves and Tournon: Syrah with up to 10 per cent Marsanne and Roussanne, lighter and earlier than Hermitage, plus white.

places.name: Crozes-Hermitage
places.note: The largest northern appellation, on flatter alluvial land around the hill: approachable Syrah with up to 15 per cent white, and the valley's best value, with Marsanne-led whites.

places.name: Hermitage
places.note: One hill behind Tain-l'Hermitage on the east bank, granite at its western end, its lieux-dits Les Bessards, Le Méal and L'Hermite: Syrah of power and decades of life with up to 15 per cent Marsanne and Roussanne, a great white, and vin de paille.

places.name: Cornas
places.note: A warm granite amphitheatre on the west bank: Syrah alone, red alone, dark and rugged, the one northern cru that admits no white grape.

places.name: Saint-Péray
places.note: The southern end of the north: Marsanne and Roussanne, still and traditional method sparkling.

places.name: Diois
places.note: Up the Drôme: Clairette de Die by the ancestral method, Muscat-led and gently sweet; Crémant de Die led by Clairette; Châtillon-en-Diois for still wine.

places.name: Southern Rhône
places.note: From Montélimar to Avignon and across the river to the Gard: Mediterranean, mistral-swept, Grenache-led blends on galets, sand and limestone, with the crus ringing the Dentelles and the papal city.

places.name: Côtes du Rhône and Côtes du Rhône Villages
places.note: The base of the ladder, almost all of it southern; Villages adds lower yields and more Grenache, and a listed commune may put its name on the label.

places.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
places.note: The papal village north of Avignon, whose growers wrote the first modern appellation rules in 1923 and were among the first appellations of 1936: thirteen named grapes, eighteen with colour variants, Grenache leading; red and white, no rosé; the embossed bottle with the papal keys.

places.name: La Crau
places.note: The high plateau of galets roulés east of the village, the stony heartland of the appellation.

places.name: Gigondas
places.note: Under the Dentelles de Montmirail on limestone scree, a cru since 1971: Grenache-led red of depth, a little rosé, and white from the 2023 vintage, Clairette at least 70 per cent, approved by the INAO in September 2022.

places.name: Vacqueyras
places.note: Gigondas's neighbour on lower, warmer ground, a cru since 1990: red, white and rosé, the red Grenache-led and slightly rounder.

places.name: Beaumes-de-Venise
places.note: Both a red cru, since 2005, and the home of Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise, the sweet fortified Muscat; the Domaine de Durban makes both.

places.name: Rasteau
places.note: Grenache vin doux naturel in several styles, rancio among them, since 1944, and a cru for dry red since 2010.

places.name: Cairanne
places.note: A cru from the 2015 vintage, red and white, the most recent promotion before Laudun; supple, spicy Grenache blends.

places.name: Vinsobres
places.note: The northernmost southern cru, in the Drôme, red only, promoted in 2006; Syrah plays a larger part here.

places.name: Lirac
places.note: On the west bank in the Gard, Tavel's neighbour: red, white and rosé, the reds in the Châteauneuf mould at a fraction of the price.

places.name: Tavel
places.note: Rosé and nothing else: Grenache and Cinsault with friends, deep in colour, dry, full and made for the table.

places.name: Laudun
places.note: Promoted to cru by the INAO on 11 September 2024 for the 2024 vintage, on the west bank in the Gard: red and white only, with a white share near a third, large for the south.

places.name: Ventoux, Luberon and Costières de Nîmes
places.note: The satellites: Ventoux on the mountain's cooler slopes, Luberon to the south, Costières de Nîmes across the Gard towards the Camargue; Grenache blends in all three colours.

places.name: Grignan-les-Adhémar
places.note: The old Coteaux du Tricastin, renamed in 2010, between the two zones in the Drôme.

producers.name: E. Guigal
producers.why: The house of Ampuis whose single-vineyard Côte-Rôties La Mouline, La Landonne and La Turque made the appellation famous worldwide.

producers.name: Domaine Jean-Louis Chave
producers.why: Hermitage's greatest grower, red and white, with vines in Mauves since the fifteenth century.

producers.name: M. Chapoutier
producers.why: Tain négociant and biodynamic domaine with single-site Hermitage such as Le Pavillon, labels in Braille.

producers.name: Paul Jaboulet Aîné
producers.why: Maker of Hermitage La Chapelle, the wine that defined the hill for a century.

producers.name: Domaine Auguste Clape
producers.why: The traditional reference for Cornas, Syrah at its most rugged and pure.

producers.name: Thierry Allemand
producers.why: Cornas grower of the low-sulphur, whole-bunch school whose wines are collected.

producers.name: Domaine Jamet
producers.why: Côte-Rôtie assembled from many parcels across both slopes, the classic grower's blend.

producers.name: Domaine René Rostaing
producers.why: Côte-Rôtie from old vines on the Côte Blonde and the Landonne; Ampodium is the house blend.

producers.name: Domaine Georges Vernay
producers.why: The domaine that saved Condrieu from disappearing in the 1950s and 1960s.

producers.name: Domaine André Perret
producers.why: Condrieu and Saint-Joseph from Chavanay, a model of ripe but balanced Viognier.

producers.name: Domaine Alain Graillot
producers.why: The grower who showed Crozes-Hermitage could be serious, whole-bunch Syrah from the plain.

producers.name: Domaine Pierre Gonon
producers.why: Saint-Joseph from the old terraces of Mauves, the appellation's benchmark.

producers.name: Château-Grillet
producers.why: The one-estate appellation of Viognier inside Condrieu.

producers.name: Château de Beaucastel
producers.why: Châteauneuf estate at Courthézon that uses all thirteen grapes, Mourvèdre prominent, and makes the Hommage à Jacques Perrin.

producers.name: Château Rayas
producers.why: All-Grenache Châteauneuf from sandy soils among pines, pale, perfumed and the cult of the south.

producers.name: Domaine du Vieux Télégraphe
producers.why: Châteauneuf from the stony plateau of La Crau, Grenache-led and built to age.

producers.name: Domaine du Pégaü
producers.why: Traditional, savoury Châteauneuf whose Cuvée Réservée is the house style.

producers.name: Clos des Papes
producers.why: Châteauneuf blended across many parcels in both colours, with a famous white.

producers.name: Henri Bonneau
producers.why: Old-school Châteauneuf whose Réserve des Célestins is a legend of long ageing in ancient casks.

producers.name: Château de Saint Cosme
producers.why: Gigondas grower and négociant with Roman-era cellars.

producers.name: Domaine Raspail-Ay
producers.why: Classic, unhurried Gigondas raised in large old wood.

producers.name: Domaine Saint-Damien
producers.why: Old-vine Gigondas from named parcels such as La Louisianne.

producers.name: Domaine de Durban
producers.why: Beaumes-de-Venise estate that makes both the red cru and the Muscat.

producers.name: Domaine de Châteaumar
producers.why: Côtes du Rhône grower whose Cuvée Vincent shows how juicy the base tier can be.

exam: The northern crus in order and the white grape each may co-ferment.
Cornas against Côte-Rôtie: all Syrah against Syrah with Viognier.
Châteauneuf-du-Pape: thirteen grapes, galets, the 1923 rules, the bottle.
The southern ladder and the crus that drop the Rhône from the label.
Tavel is rosé only; Beaumes-de-Venise and Rasteau fortify.
Hermitage against Crozes-Hermitage: the hill against the plain.
The recent promotions and their vintages: Cairanne 2015, Gigondas white 2023, Laudun 2024.
traps: Cornas admits no white grape; Côte-Rôtie may co-ferment Viognier.
Château-Grillet is a single estate with its own appellation inside Condrieu.
Crozes-Hermitage is the largest northern appellation, not a lesser part of Hermitage.
Tavel makes no red or white; its whole appellation is rosé.
The white grapes go into the vat with Syrah; blending finished wines afterwards is not allowed.
Châteauneuf-du-Pape makes red and white but no rosé.
Hermitage Blanc exists and ages for decades; Cornas Blanc does not exist.
Côtes du Rhône is legally both zones, but nearly all of it is southern.

cards.f: The northern Rhône crus, north to south
cards.b: Côte-Rôtie, Condrieu (with Château-Grillet inside), Saint-Joseph, Crozes-Hermitage, Hermitage, Cornas, Saint-Péray.

cards.f: White grapes allowed in northern Rhône reds
cards.b: Côte-Rôtie up to 20 per cent Viognier; Hermitage and Crozes up to 15 per cent Marsanne and Roussanne; Saint-Joseph 10 per cent; Cornas none. All co-fermented.
Thirteen named varieties, eighteen with colour variants: Grenache leads, with Syrah, Mourvèdre, Cinsault, Counoise, and whites such as Clairette, Bourboulenc and Roussanne.
Côtes du Rhône, Côtes du Rhône Villages, Villages with a named commune, then the crus, which drop the regional name.
Both on the west bank. Tavel is rosé only; Lirac makes red, white and rosé.
Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise (Muscat) and Rasteau (Grenache): fermentation stopped with grape spirit, a step called mutage.

cards.f: The crus and changes of the south since 2006
cards.b: Vinsobres 2006, Rasteau dry wine 2010, Cairanne from 2015, Gigondas white from 2023, Laudun from 2024.
La Mouline on the Côte Blonde, La Landonne and La Turque on the Côte Brune, all Côte-Rôtie: the La Las.
A cold, dry northerly wind down the valley: it dries canopies, cuts rot, stresses vines and forces low bush training or staking.
Hermitage is one steep hill above Tain, small and long-lived; Crozes is the big appellation on the flatter land around it.

questions.q: Which northern Rhône appellation permits Syrah alone, with no white grape in the vat?
questions.exp: Cornas is red only and Syrah only. Côte-Rôtie may co-ferment Viognier, Hermitage and Saint-Joseph a share of Marsanne and Roussanne.

questions.q: Up to what share of Viognier may be co-fermented into Côte-Rôtie?
questions.exp: Côte-Rôtie allows up to 20 per cent Viognier, fermented with the Syrah; 15 per cent is the Hermitage and Crozes figure for Marsanne and Roussanne, 10 per cent the Saint-Joseph one.

questions.q: Which southern Rhône cru makes rosé and nothing else?
questions.exp: Tavel's entire appellation is dry rosé. Lirac next door makes all three colours; Gigondas and Vacqueyras are red-led crus under the Dentelles.

questions.q: Which appellation produces a fortified sweet Muscat, a vin doux naturel, in the southern Rhône?
questions.exp: Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise is the valley's Muscat vin doux naturel; Rasteau makes the Grenache one. The other three are dry crus.

questions.q: What are the heat-holding rounded stones that cover parts of Châteauneuf-du-Pape called?
questions.exp: The galets roulés are quartzite stones rounded by the ancient Rhône; they soak up the day's heat and release it at night, and lie thickest on the plateau of La Crau.

questions.q: Which grape alone makes the white wine of Condrieu?
questions.exp: Condrieu is Viognier only, dry and perfumed with apricot; the same grape is the sole variety of Château-Grillet and the minority partner in Côte-Rôtie.

questions.q: Which colours of wine may Châteauneuf-du-Pape produce?
questions.exp: Châteauneuf-du-Pape is red and white, with no rosé permitted; Grenache leads the red, and the white draws on Clairette, Grenache Blanc, Roussanne and Bourboulenc. Tavel, across the river, is the rosé cru.

questions.q: Which Rhône village was approved as a cru by the INAO in September 2024, for red and white wine only?
questions.exp: The INAO approved Laudun, on the west bank in the Gard, as a cru on 11 September 2024 from the 2024 vintage; the cru takes no rosé.
